shortExplanation: The negative exponent makes a reciprocal, giving one quarter.
commonMistakes: Treating the negative exponent as an additional minus sign.
difficultyNotes: The parentheses keep the negative base together.

shortExplanation: Two tasks take 100 minutes, so each takes 50 minutes.
detailedSteps: The interval from 1:00 PM to 2:40 PM is 100 minutes. Two equal tasks occupy it, so the third takes another 50 minutes and ends at 3:30 PM.
commonMistakes: Dividing the observed interval by three tasks.
difficultyNotes: Count the completed tasks in the given interval.

shortExplanation: Only three copies of 28 leave an integer for the other number.
detailedSteps: If 28 occurs twice, the other integer would be $(100-56)/3=44/3$, which is not an integer.
Thus 28 occurs three times, and the other integer is $(100-84)/2=8$.
commonMistakes: Assuming which number appears twice without checking integrality.
difficultyNotes: The integer condition resolves the ambiguity.

shortExplanation: Dan gets thirteen sixtieths, between Cyril and Alex.
detailedSteps: In sixtieths, Alex eats 12, Beth 20, and Cyril 15. Dan gets $60-12-20-15=13$.
The decreasing order is therefore Beth, Cyril, Dan, Alex.
commonMistakes: Ranking the leftovers without calculating them.
difficultyNotes: A common denominator makes the ordering immediate.

shortExplanation: Working backward from Marta puts Hikmet eighth.
detailedSteps: Marta is sixth, so Jack is fifth, Todd is third, and Rand is second.
Hikmet is six places behind Rand, hence eighth. David is two places behind Hikmet, hence tenth.
commonMistakes: Reversing ahead and behind in one of the relations.
difficultyNotes: Use the anchored finishing place first.

shortExplanation: Tennis must be Thursday, forcing swimming on Saturday.
detailedSteps: The day before tennis cannot be running or swimming. It must therefore be basketball or golf, so tennis is Tuesday or Thursday.
If tennis were Tuesday, three runs would have to lie among Thursday through Sunday, impossible without consecutive days. Therefore tennis is Thursday.
The remaining days are Tuesday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. Three nonconsecutive runs must be Tuesday, Friday and Sunday; swimming is Saturday.
commonMistakes: Ignoring the restriction on the day immediately before tennis.
difficultyNotes: The fixed sports severely limit the possible tennis day.

shortExplanation: The two groupings give one sixth and two fifths.
detailedSteps: The left grouping is $(1-1/2)-1/3=1/6$. The right grouping is $1-1/(2-1/3)=1-3/5=2/5$.
The requested difference is $1/6-2/5=-7/30$.
commonMistakes: Assuming the custom operation is associative.
difficultyNotes: Follow the parentheses before subtracting the results.

shortExplanation: The composition exchanges the x- and y-coordinates.
detailedSteps: A clockwise quarter turn maps $(x,y)$ to $(y,-x)$. Reflection in the y-axis then gives $(-y,-x)$, and the half turn gives $(y,x)$.

Thus the full operation is reflection in $y=x$. The original vertical stem becomes a horizontal stem on the positive x-axis, with its longer end arm on the right. The actual option matching these features is E.
commonMistakes: Applying the three transformations in the wrong order.
difficultyNotes: An image choice requires checking orientation as well as quadrant.

shortExplanation: Subtract the smaller right semicircle from the large quarter disk.
detailedSteps: The radius-three quarter disk has area $9\pi/4$. The removed right semicircle has radius $3/2$ and area $(1/2)\pi(3/2)^2=9\pi/8$.
The remaining area is $9\pi/4-9\pi/8=9\pi/8$.
keyIdeas: A quarter disk minus a semicircle
commonMistakes: Subtracting a full small disk instead of the visible semicircle.
difficultyNotes: The actual shading specifies which portions are removed.

shortExplanation: There are 1007 negative factors, and the absolute product ends in five.
detailedSteps: The factors are $-1,-3,\ldots,-2013$, numbering $(2013+1)/2=1007$. An odd number of negative factors gives a negative product.
Every factor is odd and one is divisible by 5. The absolute product is therefore odd and divisible by 5, so its units digit is 5.
keyIdeas: Parity and final digits of a product
commonMistakes: Including the excluded endpoint -2015.
difficultyNotes: Sign and last digit can be handled separately.

shortExplanation: Eight of the twenty eligible integers are prime.
detailedSteps: The allowed digits are $2,3,5,7$. There are four one-digit and sixteen two-digit eligible integers.
All four one-digit values are prime. The two-digit primes are $23,37,53,73$; the other candidates are even, divisible by 5, or among $27,33,57,77$.
The probability is $(4+4)/(4+16)=2/5$.
commonMistakes: Counting every number with prime digits as a prime number.
difficultyNotes: Include the one-digit integers in the sample space.

shortExplanation: The circle condition reduces to x squared at most 25.
detailedSteps: The squared distance is $(x-5)^2+(-x-5)^2=2x^2+50$. Being inside or on the circle means $2x^2+50\le100$, hence $-5\le x\le5$.
There are eleven integers in this inclusive interval.
keyIdeas: Integer points in a translated circle
commonMistakes: Dropping the boundary points or using the wrong translated coordinates.
difficultyNotes: The linear terms cancel along the line y=-x.

shortExplanation: The legs are 5 and 12, and the third altitude is 60/13.
detailedSteps: The intercepts are $(5,0)$ and $(0,12)$, making a right triangle with hypotenuse 13 and area 30.
Two altitudes are the perpendicular legs, 5 and 12. The altitude to the hypotenuse is $2(30)/13=60/13$.
keyIdeas: Three altitudes of an intercept triangle
commonMistakes: Adding side lengths in place of the altitudes.
difficultyNotes: One altitude is shorter than either leg.

shortExplanation: Give the largest digit to the root with coefficient one.
detailedSteps: The equation factors as $(x-b)(2x-a-c)=0$, so the root sum is $b+(a+c)/2$.
Among three distinct digits, the largest three are 9,8,7. Since b has twice the weight of either other digit, the maximum assigns $b=9$ and $\{a,c\}=\{8,7\}$.
The maximum is $9+(8+7)/2=33/2$.
keyIdeas: Factoring to optimize a root sum
commonMistakes: Assigning the largest digit to a lower-weight variable.
difficultyNotes: An exchange argument justifies the optimal assignment.

shortExplanation: Every possible total has the form 13 h+5 c.
detailedSteps: For h horses there are 3 h people and 9 h ducks, totaling 13 h. For c cows there are 4 c sheep, totaling 5 c. Thus the full total is $13h+5c$.
If this equals 47, reduction modulo 5 gives $h\equiv4\pmod5$. The least nonnegative such h is 4, already contributing 52, so 47 is impossible.
commonMistakes: Omitting the ducks or counting sheep without cows.
difficultyNotes: A congruence rules out the exceptional value without guessing populations.

shortExplanation: There are nine valid ordered chains among 720 assignments.
detailedSteps: Distinct positive multiples force $C<B<A$. If $C=1$, the choices $B=2,3,4,5$ permit respectively 4,2,1,1 choices for A, giving eight chains.
If $C=2$, only $B=4,A=8$ works. If $C\ge3$, then $B\ge2C$ and $A\ge2B\ge12$, impossible.
All $10\cdot9\cdot8=720$ distinct assignments are equally likely, so the probability is $9/720=1/80$.
commonMistakes: Allowing two people to receive the same number.
difficultyNotes: The lower bounds on successive multiples keep the count small.

shortExplanation: Two pyramids share a rhombus of area ten.
detailedSteps: Use the source prism dimensions 3,4,5. The four side-face centers form a rhombus with diagonals 4 and 5, so its area is $4\cdot5/2=10$.
The top and bottom face centers form the two apices. Their heights above and below the rhombus plane total 3, giving volume $(1/3)\cdot10\cdot3=10$.
commonMistakes: Using the full prism volume or assuming a regular octahedron.
difficultyNotes: The face-center octahedron need not be regular.

shortExplanation: Each coin is heads eventually with probability seven eighths.
detailedSteps: A coin is left tails only if all three permitted flips are tails, with probability $1/8$. Its final heads probability is therefore $7/8$.
Linearity of expectation gives $64\cdot7/8=56$. Independence between final indicators is not needed for this expectation calculation.
commonMistakes: Counting only heads on the final round of flips.
difficultyNotes: Once heads occurs, that coin stays heads.

shortExplanation: The cyclic condition forces the two legs to be equal.
detailedSteps: Place $C=(0,0),A=(a,0),B=(0,b)$, with $a,b>0$. The outside squares give $W=(0,-a),Z=(a,-a),X=(b,a+b),Y=(a+b,a)$.
The circle through W and Z has center $(a/2,t)$. Equating squared distances to Z and Y gives $4at=b(a+b)$. Equating them to Z and X gives $2(2a+b)t=b(a+2b)$.
Eliminating t yields $(a+b)(2a+b)=2a(a+2b)$, hence $b^2=ab$ and $a=b$.
Since $a^2+b^2=12^2$, both legs are $6\sqrt2$. The perimeter is $12+12\sqrt2$.
keyIdeas: Cyclic vertices from two exterior squares
commonMistakes: Placing one square inside the triangle, which changes its other vertices.
difficultyNotes: Coordinates enforce the outside-square orientation explicitly.

shortExplanation: The endpoint must be the opposite corner, and the first two edges determine the path.
detailedSteps: Label vertices by three bits, starting at 000. Each edge changes bit parity, so after seven edges the endpoint has odd parity. To be nonadjacent to the start, it must be 111.
The first edge has three choices, and the second has two choices because returning is forbidden. Relabel axes to make the prefix $000,001,011$.

The required endpoint cannot be visited early. The remaining path is then forced: $010,110,100,101,111$. At each intermediate vertex the other available edge returns to a visited vertex or reaches 111 too early.
Thus there are $3\cdot2=6$ paths.
commonMistakes: Counting paths that end at a neighbor of the starting corner.
difficultyNotes: Parity identifies the unique possible terminal vertex.

shortExplanation: The possible stair counts are 63,64,66.
detailedSteps: The jump counts are $\lceil N/2\rceil$ and $\lceil N/5\rceil$. Write $N=10q+r$, where $0\le r\le9$. Their difference is $3q+\lceil r/2\rceil-\lceil r/5\rceil$.
For residues 0 through 9, the last difference is $0,0,0,1,1,2,1,2,2,3$. To total 19, its residue modulo 3 must be 1, so it must equal 1 and $q=6$.
The residues are 3,4,6, giving counts 63,64,66. Their sum is 193, whose digit sum is $1+9+3=13$.
commonMistakes: Using fractional jump counts instead of rounding up.
difficultyNotes: The two jump lengths share period ten in their remainder behavior.

shortExplanation: The three requested lengths are 1/phi, 1 and phi.
detailedSteps: Let the outer side be s, its diagonal d, and $\phi=(1+\sqrt5)/2$. Ptolemy in cyclic quadrilateral ABCD gives $d^2=s^2+sd$, so $d/s=\phi$.

The regular-pentagon angles make triangle ABG have equal 36-degree angles at A and B, giving $BG=AG=1$. Triangle BCG has equal 72-degree angles at B and G, giving $CG=BC=s$. Hence $d=AC=1+s$ and $s=\phi$.
Triangles AFG and CBG have corresponding angles 36,72,72. Therefore $FG/BG=AG/CG=1/\phi$, giving $FG=1/\phi$.
The five inner intersection points form a regular pentagon by rotational symmetry. Its side is FG, while JH is a diagonal, so $JH=\phi FG=1$.
Finally $FG+JH+CD=1/\phi+1+\phi=2\phi=1+\sqrt5$.
commonMistakes: Treating JH as a side of the inner pentagon.
difficultyNotes: Use the exact source labels to distinguish inner sides and diagonals.

shortExplanation: The first four eligible integers are 8,9,13,14.
detailedSteps: The number of trailing zeros is $Z(n)=\lfloor n/5\rfloor+\lfloor n/25\rfloor+\cdots$.
For $5\le n\le14$, $Z(n)=\lfloor n/5\rfloor$, while $Z(2n)=\lfloor2n/5\rfloor+\lfloor2n/25\rfloor$. Checking these short intervals, the equality $Z(2n)=3Z(n)$ holds at exactly $n=8,9,13,14$.
There are already four solutions by 14, so these are the four least permitted values. Their sum is 44, with digit sum 8.
commonMistakes: Omitting the extra factor of 5 from the multiple 25 in (2 n)!.
difficultyNotes: Only a finite initial interval is needed to identify the four least values.

shortExplanation: Index 2015 lies 35 steps east of the lower-left corner of layer 22.
detailedSteps: The successive straight runs have lengths $1,1,2,2,3,3,\ldots$. Completing layer r ends at $(r,-r)$ at index $(2r+1)^2-1$.
Index 2015 is 35 steps east of that last corner, so its coordinates are $(-22+35,-22)=(13,-22)$.
keyIdeas: Locating an index in a square spiral
commonMistakes: Shifting the index by one because the origin is p 0.
difficultyNotes: The spiral rule fixes both the orientation and the corner indices.

shortExplanation: A reciprocal identity bounds both smaller dimensions.
detailedSteps: Dividing $abc=2(ab+ac+bc)$ by $2abc$ gives $1/a+1/b+1/c=1/2$. Positivity and $a\le b\le c$ imply $3\le a\le6$.
Solving for c gives $c=2ab/(ab-2a-2b)$. A positive denominator requires $b>2a/(a-2)$, and $c\ge b$ requires $b\le4a/(a-2)$.
These bounds leave b ranges 7 through 12 for a=3, 5 through 8 for a=4, 5 through 6 for a=5, and only 6 for a=6.
The total is $5+3+1+1=10$. Each listed triple meets the original equality and ordering.
keyIdeas: Integer boxes with equal area and volume
commonMistakes: Counting permutations despite the imposed sorted order, or searching without a complete bound.
difficultyNotes: The ordering converts the reciprocal equation into a finite search.
